bull_thesis: The bull case is that a signed, binding sale rescues a balance sheet the market has written off, and the freight-rail platform left behind gets valued like the scarce asset it is. On 30 April 2026 FTAI Infrastructure agreed to sell Long Ridge Energy and Power -- a 485-to-505 megawatt gas-fired plant at Hannibal, Ohio, gas-well interests, and about 1,600 contiguous acres on the Ohio River -- to a subsidiary of MARA Holdings for roughly $1.52 billion. The buyer is committed and visibly still building in the same direction: it secured consents from holders of its 8.75% senior notes in June 2026 to permit the purchase, funded its infrastructure push partly by selling about $1.5 billion of bitcoin, and signed for a further 1,200-acre powered site in Texas on 9 July 2026. Closing takes total debt from $3.814 billion to $2.377 billion, parent-company debt from $1.310 billion to $1.019 billion, and corporate leverage (debt measured against earnings) from 9.5 times to 7.4 times, while handing the company more than $300 million of net cash that repays parent debt carrying a 9.75% coupon and saves about $30 million a year of interest. Management has already said Jefferson and Repauno are the next assets out the door within twelve to eighteen months, with roughly $700 million of proceeds pre-assigned to parent debt -- a sequenced path to the stated 5.1 times leverage target. Underneath sits a business that is working: the rail segment (Transtar plus Wheeling and Lake Erie) earned $40.2 million in the first quarter of 2026, up 31% on the same quarter a year earlier, and short-line and regional railroads are local franchises a competitor cannot rebuild. Management's near-term earnings target of $278 million excluding Long Ridge is built from an annualised first-quarter run rate of about $176 million, plus $13 million of rail integration synergies, $9 million of new Jefferson terminal contracts, and $80 million once Repauno phase two commissions. Because the capital structure is so heavy, the equity is extremely geared to the multiple applied to those earnings: capitalising $278 million at sixteen times and deducting $2.38 billion of pro-forma debt and the roughly $1.4 billion rail-holding-company preferred claim leaves about $5.50 a share; at seventeen times, about $7.87; at eighteen times, about $10.20. Three analysts publish targets between $8.75 and $12. The conditions this requires are specific and all must hold: the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission grants the change-of-control approval without crippling conditions, the deal closes and the cash is actually applied to the 9.75% term loan, Repauno phase two reaches mechanical completion in autumn 2026 and begins operating in the first quarter of 2027 as guided, and infrastructure multiples stay near seventeen times.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is a leveraged option with no floor, and the option is already going against us. The downside level this position was scored against, $3.90, broke in the last week of July 2026: the shares closed at $3.73 on 31 July, down 6.75% that day, at a new 52-week low of $3.71, after falling five sessions in a row and eight of the last ten -- roughly 13% over that stretch and about 37% over twelve months. The stock is falling into the catalyst rather than tightening toward it, which is the opposite of what a defined-risk event setup should do. Structurally the common shareholder is at the very back of a very long queue. After the sale closes, roughly $2.38 billion of debt sits ahead of the equity, and above that again is a preferred stake at the rail holding company: about $1 billion sold to funds managed by Ares Management to finance the Wheeling and Lake Erie purchase, carried at $970.5 million on 31 March 2026, redeemable at $1,417.49 per share (about $1.4 billion in total), with dividends paid in kind so the claim compounds rather than being paid in cash, and no redemption obligation until 25 August 2032. That is close to $3.8 billion of senior claims against an equity market value of about $441 million. Book equity attributable to the company was already negative $303.1 million at 31 March 2026, unrestricted cash was $37.9 million, and the first-quarter filing carries the standard formulation of going-concern doubt resolved by pointing at the pending sale: planned actions are considered probable to be implemented and to provide sufficient liquidity to meet obligations. Take the sale away and that sentence has to be rewritten. The sale itself is not a value unlock -- $1.52 billion for an asset generating about $144 million of annualised earnings in the second half of 2025 is roughly eleven times, a fair price, so the transaction is close to neutral on enterprise value and matters almost entirely for liquidity. Meanwhile the largest single block of the earnings target, the $80 million from Repauno phase two, is a construction project that produced negative $2.3 million in the first quarter of 2026 and does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027 -- after the event window closes. On today's realistic earnings power of roughly $198 million, once rail synergies and Jefferson contracts land but before Repauno contributes, the common is worth close to nothing at any conventional infrastructure multiple; at fifteen times it is negative. Behaviour reinforces the concern: the $45 million Tidewater Logistics purchase on 29 June 2026 was funded by upsizing the term loan, adding parent debt inside a deleveraging quarter, and the 1 July 2026 Jefferson refinancing replaced $217.9 million of bonds with a $230 million bridge loan due 30 June 2027 rather than removing the maturity. The first quarter of 2026 lost $1.32 a share against a consensus near $0.35. Moody's rates the company B3 with a negative outlook. And the regulatory path is not clear: the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments on 29 May 2026 urging that the deal not be approved without a commitment from the buyer not to remove Long Ridge capacity from PJM markets to serve data-centre load, and no approval order had been published as of 3 August 2026. What confirms the bear case: a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order with output-commitment conditions that reduce the asset's value to the buyer, any slip past the contractual outside date of 30 November 2026 toward the 30 June 2027 regulatory backstop, a Repauno commissioning delay, or a cut to the three-cent quarterly dividend.
sop_bull: About $8.00 to $10.20 a share. Method: capitalise management's near-term target of $278 million of adjusted earnings excluding Long Ridge -- built as roughly $176 million annualised first-quarter run rate, plus $13 million rail integration synergies, plus $9 million new Jefferson contracts, plus $80 million from Repauno phase two -- at seventeen to eighteen times, the range implied by the published analyst targets of $8.75 to $12. Seventeen times gives an enterprise value of $4.73 billion; eighteen times gives $5.00 billion. Deduct pro-forma total debt of $2.38 billion (management's own post-close figure) and the rail-holding-company preferred claim of about $1.42 billion at its stated redemption value, then divide by 118.2 million shares outstanding: $7.87 at seventeen times, $10.20 at eighteen. Sense-check by the parts: rail at about $174 million of run-rate earnings on sixteen times is roughly $2.78 billion, Jefferson at about $58 million on twelve times is roughly $0.70 billion, a fully commissioned Repauno at $80 million on thirteen times is roughly $1.04 billion, Tidewater about $0.06 billion, less capitalised corporate overhead -- which sums to the same neighbourhood. The dominant sensitivity is the multiple, not the earnings: because senior claims are so large relative to the equity, each single turn of multiple is worth about $2.35 a share.
sop_bear: About $0.40 to $1.75 a share, and there is no verified structural floor above zero. Method: value the operating businesses on earnings power that exists today rather than on the completed-construction target. Once rail integration synergies and the new Jefferson contracts land but before Repauno phase two contributes anything, run-rate earnings are roughly $198 million. At fifteen times that is $2.97 billion of enterprise value against roughly $3.80 billion of pro-forma debt ($2.38 billion) plus the rail preferred claim ($1.42 billion) -- the common is worth nothing. Even at twenty times, a multiple no distressed infrastructure holding company commands, the residual is about $1.35 a share. The severe case, in which the sale slips toward the 30 June 2027 regulatory backstop or breaks, is worse still: book equity is already negative $303.1 million, unrestricted cash was $37.9 million at 31 March 2026, the going-concern assessment is expressly supported by the pending sale, the term loan costs 9.75% and matures February 2028, and a $230 million Jefferson bridge loan comes due 30 June 2027. In that path the equity is a residual claim behind about $3.8 billion, worth perhaps $0.40, and dilution or a restructuring becomes the live question. The point that governs the decision: the $3.90 level this candidate was scored against as a floor is not a floor -- it was simply the prior 52-week low, and it broke on 29-31 July 2026.
sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across four paths, because the payoff is driven by the multiple and by Repauno rather than by the deal alone. Path one, 35% weight: the sale closes in the third or fourth quarter of 2026, Repauno phase two commissions on schedule in the first quarter of 2027, and the market capitalises the $278 million target near sixteen to seventeen times -- about $6.50 a share. Path two, 35%: the sale closes, but Repauno slips or the multiple holds near fifteen times -- about $3.00. Path three, 20%: the sale closes late or with Federal Energy Regulatory Commission conditions attached, liquidity stays tight, and the dividend or the share count gives -- about $1.75. Path four, 10%: the deal slips toward the 30 June 2027 backstop or breaks, the going-concern question reopens and restructuring risk becomes live -- about $0.40. Weighted, that is $3.72 a share. The parts underneath: freight rail (Transtar plus Wheeling and Lake Erie) is the only segment carrying real, durable value at roughly $2.4 to $2.8 billion of enterprise value; Jefferson terminal roughly $0.6 to $0.7 billion; Repauno is worth about $1.0 billion once commissioned and close to its build cost before that; Tidewater about $0.06 billion. Against that sits $2.38 billion of pro-forma debt and about $1.42 billion of compounding rail preferred, which together consume essentially all of it. The market value of $441 million on 118.2 million shares is, on this arithmetic, close to fair -- which is precisely the problem for a candidate selected for asymmetry.
risk_reward: Roughly 2.3 to 1 measured endpoint to endpoint, but that ratio flatters the setup and should not be relied on. Upside to a realistic event-resolved target of $8.75 is about +135% from $3.73; downside to a bear value of $1.50 is about -60%. The problem is that the downside is not bounded at $1.50 by anything contractual or structural -- it is an estimate, not a floor. The level actually scored as the floor, $3.90, broke on 29-31 July 2026 and the shares are now below it at a 52-week low. With roughly $3.8 billion of debt and compounding preferred ahead of a $441 million equity stub, negative book equity, and going-concern language supported by the pending sale, the true downside is zero. Probability-weighted fair value of about $3.70 sits essentially on top of the $3.73 price, so the expected return today is close to nil with a fat tail in each direction. This is a leveraged option, not a defined-risk trade.
catalyst_summary: Binding sale of the Long Ridge power business to MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion, guided to close in the third quarter of 2026 with a contractual outside date of 30 November 2026 -- real and dated, but it buys survival rather than a re-rating, and the downside level the position was scored against has already broken.
dated_milestone: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approval of the change of control under section 203 of the Federal Power Act, docket EC26-92-000, filed 8 May 2026 with comments closed 29 May 2026 and no order published as of 3 August 2026. Management guides to approval in the middle of the third quarter of 2026 and a close in the third quarter; the purchase agreement's contractual outside date is 30 November 2026, extending to 30 June 2027 if regulatory conditions remain unsatisfied. Nearer dated events: second-quarter results after the close on 5 August 2026, and the buyer's results on 6 August 2026, either of which can update the closing timeline within days.
forcing_function: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order in docket EC26-92-000, followed by the actual closing and the application of more than $300 million of net proceeds against parent debt carrying a 9.75% coupon. That sequence is what converts an accounting going-concern question into a funded balance sheet and gives the market permission to capitalise the rail platform at an infrastructure multiple. It is genuinely dated and genuinely binding, with a termination right for either party if the deal has not closed by 30 November 2026 and a regulatory extension to 30 June 2027. Two things qualify it. First, the 30 September 2026 date this candidate was scored on is management's guidance, not the contract -- a slip into the fourth quarter is permitted and would not break the deal, only the timing assumption. Second, the approval is contested: the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments on 29 May 2026 asking that the transaction not be approved without a commitment from the buyer not to remove Long Ridge capacity and energy from PJM markets to serve data-centre load, and that monitor has opposed comparable power-plant-to-data-centre acquisitions before. The realistic risk there is conditions and delay rather than denial. Note also what this event is not: the company is the seller, not the target, so there is no offer price for its own shares, no arbitrage spread, and no bid underneath the stock -- which is exactly why the shares fell about 13% in ten sessions while the deal remained fully on track.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not about whether the deal closes -- the market broadly expects it to, and so do we. The disagreement is about what closing is worth. The published targets of $8.75 (JonesTrading, initiated 1 July 2026), $10 (Citizens JMP, cut from $12 on 15 July 2026) and up to $12 imply capitalising management's $278 million near-term earnings target at roughly seventeen to eighteen times. Two assumptions inside that are, on the evidence, wrong or at least unearned. First, the target is treated as a near-term number when management's own build makes $80 million of it -- nearly a third -- dependent on Repauno phase two, which reaches mechanical completion in autumn 2026 and begins commissioning and operations in the first quarter of 2027, and which lost $2.3 million in the first quarter of 2026. On the earnings that will actually exist when the deal closes, roughly $198 million, seventeen times leaves the common worth nothing after senior claims. Second, and more important, the sell-side framing consistently under-weights the rail-holding-company preferred: about $1 billion placed with funds managed by Ares Management, carried at $970.5 million, redeemable at $1,417.49 per share for roughly $1.4 billion, with dividends paid in kind so it compounds ahead of the common and is not repayable until 25 August 2032. Deduct it at redemption value and roughly $2.35 a share of equity value disappears for every turn of multiple you have to give back. Where the market is right and the bulls have a point is that the deal is real, the buyer is committed and still buying adjacent assets, and the rail business is compounding at 31% year on year. Where our own board entry was wrong is the floor: $3.90 was never a structural level, only the prior 52-week low, and it broke on 29-31 July 2026.
valley_of_death: The risky window is the next three to nine months and it is unusually well defined. First, the approval itself: no Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order had been published as of 3 August 2026, with a live protest from the PJM market monitor asking for output commitments as a condition. A conditioned approval is the most likely adverse outcome and would slow the close; the contract permits slippage to 30 November 2026 and, on regulatory grounds, to 30 June 2027. Every month of delay is another month of a 9.75% term loan coupon against $37.9 million of unrestricted cash. Second, liquidity between here and the close: the company is loss-making at the bottom line -- a $127.2 million net loss and $1.32 loss per share in the first quarter of 2026 against a consensus near $0.35 -- with negative book equity of $303.1 million and going-concern comfort in the filings that rests explicitly on this sale completing. Third, a maturity that has been moved rather than removed: the 1 July 2026 Jefferson refinancing replaced $217.9 million of 2024-vintage revenue bonds with a $230 million secured bridge loan from Jefferies Finance due 30 June 2027. That has to be termed out inside a year, into whatever credit market exists then, on a B3-rated negative-outlook borrower. Fourth, capital discipline drift: the $45 million Tidewater Logistics acquisition on 29 June 2026 was funded by upsizing the term loan, adding parent debt in the middle of a deleveraging story -- a pattern worth watching, because more of it would undo the point of the sale. Fifth, the two immediate information events: second-quarter results on 5 August 2026 and the buyer's results on 6 August 2026. Either can move the closing timeline, and given the stock is already at a 52-week low on a five-session losing streak, the market is not positioned for good news.
positioning_washout: The forced-selling picture is thin rather than dramatic, which is itself a warning. This is a roughly $441 million company on 118.2 million shares -- too small for meaningful index demand and small enough that a single fund exiting moves it. The most likely mechanical seller is the income base: the company still pays a three-cent quarterly dividend that is a rounding error against a 9.75% term loan, and it is by far the cheapest line item to cut if the closing timeline slips. A cut would push out whatever yield-oriented holders remain, most of whom bought this as a spin-out from a dividend-paying parent. Rating-driven selling has already partly happened: Moody's rates the company B3 with a negative outlook, Wall Street Zen moved to its strongest sell rating on 21 July 2026, and Citizens JMP cut its target from $12 to $10 on 15 July 2026 while keeping a positive rating. The five-session decline into a 52-week low at $3.71 on 31 July 2026 has the texture of position liquidation ahead of the 5 August results rather than a clean capitulation -- there is no volume spike or single-day flush that would mark a washout low. The absence of a completed flush is precisely why waiting has value here: the shareholder base has not yet been cleared, and there is no natural bid, because the company is the seller in this transaction and its own shares carry no offer price.
moderator_conclusion: This is a real, binding, dated event attached to the wrong side of a capital structure, and it should not be sized as the asymmetric special situation it was screened as. Everything on the event leg checks out: a definitive agreement signed 30 April 2026 to sell the Long Ridge power business to MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion, a committed buyer that has cleared its own bondholder consents and keeps acquiring adjacent power assets, proper advisers on both sides, a filed regulatory application, and a contractual termination date of 30 November 2026 with a regulatory extension to 30 June 2027. Management has executed the financing plan competently -- refinancing a bridge into a $1.35 billion term loan, closing the Wheeling and Lake Erie acquisition and delivering 31% rail earnings growth, refinancing the Jefferson bonds. What fails is the risk leg, and it fails on verified facts rather than judgement. The level this position was underwritten against as a floor, $3.90, broke in the last week of July 2026; the shares closed at $3.73 on 31 July at a new 52-week low of $3.71, having fallen five sessions running. There is nothing structural beneath that price: book equity is negative $303.1 million, unrestricted cash was $37.9 million at 31 March 2026, the going-concern assessment leans on this very sale, and roughly $3.8 billion of debt and compounding preferred sits ahead of a $441 million equity stub -- including about $1.4 billion of rail-holding-company preferred that pays dividends in kind and is not redeemable until 2032. Because senior claims are that large, the equity swings about $2.35 a share for every single turn of the multiple applied to the operating businesses, and the entire published bull case rests on capitalising an earnings target at seventeen to eighteen times whose largest component -- $80 million from Repauno phase two -- does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027, after the event window shuts. Probability-weight the paths honestly and fair value lands at about $3.70, essentially on top of the price. That is the definition of a fairly priced option, not a mispriced spread. The right posture is to wait, and the things to wait for are specific rather than atmospheric: the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order in docket EC26-92-000 without value-destroying output conditions, the deal actually closing with more than $300 million of net proceeds visibly applied to the 9.75% parent term loan, and confirmation at the second-quarter results on 5 August 2026 that Repauno phase two still reaches mechanical completion this autumn. Get those three and the seventeen-times case becomes underwritable and $8 to $10 is reachable. Alternatively, a price below about $2.50 would pay properly for what this actually is -- a leveraged call on infrastructure multiples over a scarce but heavily encumbered rail franchise. Buying it here, at fair value, with the floor already broken and the shares falling into the catalyst, is taking the option risk without the option price.
interrogator_dossier:
# FTAI Infrastructure Inc. (FIP) -- Event Dossier

Prepared 3 August 2026. All prices and filings verified against public sources on that date.

The one-line version: the catalyst is real and contractually binding -- a signed agreement to sell the Long Ridge power business to MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion -- but it is a survival event, not a value-unlock event, and the downside floor this candidate was scored against has already given way.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC -- what the company is trying to become

FTAI Infrastructure was spun out of Fortress Transportation in 2022 as a grab-bag of hard assets: two freight railroads (Transtar, and Wheeling & Lake Erie, bought for $1.05 billion and closed in 2025), a deepwater crude and ammonia terminal on the Texas coast (Jefferson), a natural-gas storage and export terminal on the Delaware River (Repauno), and a 485-megawatt gas-fired power plant in Ohio (Long Ridge).

Across the last four quarters the story has narrowed sharply and deliberately. Management now describes the company as a freight-rail platform that happens to be carrying two terminals and a power plant it intends to sell. Chief executive Ken Nicholson framed the Long Ridge agreement on 30 April 2026 as a key step in the strategic plan, unlocking value to shareholders and deleveraging the company. On the first-quarter call in May, management went further and named Jefferson and Repauno as the next assets out the door, within twelve to eighteen months, with roughly $700 million of the resulting cash earmarked for parent-company debt.

That is a coherent plan. It is also an admission: the company is selling assets because the balance sheet demands it, not because the market is paying a premium.

## 2. THE EVENT -- is it real, dated and binding?

Yes on real and binding; qualified on dated.

- What: a definitive equity purchase agreement, announced 30 April 2026, to sell Long Ridge Energy & Power LLC -- a 485-to-505 megawatt combined-cycle gas plant at Hannibal, Ohio, working interests in gas wells, and roughly 1,600 contiguous acres on the Ohio River -- to a subsidiary of MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion before closing adjustments.
- Who is buying: MARA Holdings, the former bitcoin miner now rebuilding itself as an artificial-intelligence data-centre and power company. Its commitment looks genuine rather than opportunistic: it has secured consents from holders of its 8.75% senior notes to permit the acquisition (June 2026), sold about $1.5 billion of bitcoin to fund its infrastructure push, and has kept buying power assets since -- a 1,200-acre powered site in Matagorda County, Texas on 9 July 2026. A buyer that keeps writing cheques for adjacent assets is not a buyer looking for a way out.
- What still has to happen: clearance under the Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust act, and approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for the change of control under section 203 of the Federal Power Act. The joint application was filed on 8 May 2026 under docket EC26-92-000, with a comment deadline of 29 May 2026. Related railroad agreements also require Surface Transportation Board coordination.
- The dates that actually bind: the purchase agreement can be terminated by either side if the deal has not closed by 30 November 2026, extending to 30 June 2027 if regulatory conditions remain outstanding. Management's guidance is a close in the third quarter of 2026, with approval in the middle of the third quarter.

This matters for how the candidate was scored. The 30 September 2026 date in our board entry is management's guidance, not a contractual deadline. The binding outside date is two months later, with a further seven-month regulatory extension available. A slip past September is permitted by the contract and would not break the deal -- but it would break the timing assumption the position was underwritten on.

The live regulatory friction: on 29 May 2026 the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission urging that the transaction not be approved without a commitment from the buyer not to remove the Long Ridge capacity and energy from PJM markets to serve data-centre load. The monitor has taken the same position against comparable power-plant-to-data-centre acquisitions before. The buyer's answer is that it intends to keep participating in PJM markets. As of 3 August 2026 no order granting the authorisation has been published. This is the single open item, and it is the kind of item that produces conditions and delay rather than outright denial -- but delay is exactly what this balance sheet cannot absorb cheaply.

## 3. THE CLAIM VERSUS THE ARITHMETIC -- where the deal money actually goes

Management's own pro-forma figures, from the first-quarter 2026 presentation: total debt falls from $3.814 billion to $2.377 billion; parent-company debt from $1.310 billion to $1.019 billion; subsidiary non-recourse debt from $2.504 billion to $1.358 billion; corporate leverage (debt measured against earnings) from 9.5 times to 7.4 times.

Net cash to the company is more than $300 million, essentially all of which repays parent debt, saving about $30 million a year of interest. The $1.16 billion of debt that disappears was borrowed against Long Ridge itself and was never a claim on the rest of the company.

Read those figures honestly. The sale takes leverage from distressed to merely very high. Management's own stated destination is 5.1 times, which the sale alone does not reach. The price paid -- $1.52 billion for an asset that generated about $144 million of annualised earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the second half of 2025, with 76% of output contracted -- works out near eleven times. That is a fair price, not a windfall. The transaction is close to value-neutral on enterprise value and enormously positive on liquidity. Anyone underwriting this as a hidden-value unlock has the wrong model of it.

Where the earnings actually have to come from. Management's near-term target is $278 million of adjusted earnings excluding Long Ridge. The build is explicit: the first quarter's run rate annualises to roughly $176 million, plus $13 million from integrating Wheeling & Lake Erie with Transtar, plus $9 million from new Jefferson contracts, plus $80 million from Repauno phase two. Repauno phase two reaches mechanical completion in autumn 2026 and begins commissioning and operations in the first quarter of 2027.

So the largest single component of the target -- nearly a third of it -- is a construction project that will not produce a dollar of earnings until after the catalyst window closes. Segment detail for the first quarter of 2026: rail $40.2 million (up 31% year on year), Jefferson $14.4 million, Long Ridge $26.4 million, Repauno negative $2.3 million, consolidated $70.6 million.

## 4. THE FLOOR -- what actually backstops the price if the event disappoints

There is no verified floor. This is the finding that should govern the decision.

- The stock closed at $3.73 on 31 July 2026, down 6.75% that day, on its 52-week low of $3.71. Our board entry carried a live price of $4.16 and a downside floor of $3.90. The price is already through the floor, roughly 4% below it, and it got there falling five sessions in a row and eight of ten, down about 13% over that stretch. Over twelve months the shares are down roughly 37%.
- The claims ahead of the common shareholder are overwhelming. Against a market value of about $441 million on 118.2 million shares sit, after the sale closes, roughly $2.38 billion of debt plus a preferred-stock claim at the rail holding company. That preferred -- about $1 billion sold to funds managed by Ares Management to finance the Wheeling & Lake Erie purchase -- carried $970.5 million on the books at 31 March 2026 and would be redeemable at $1,417.49 per share, roughly $1.4 billion in total, with dividends paid in kind (added to the balance rather than paid in cash, so the claim compounds). Its earliest redemption is 25 August 2032. Total senior claims are therefore near $3.8 billion against a $441 million equity stub.
- Book equity is already negative: total equity attributable to the company was negative $303.1 million at 31 March 2026.
- The liquidity language is the standard substantial-doubt-alleviated formulation. The first-quarter filing states that the planned sale will further improve the liquidity position and that planned actions are considered probable to be implemented and to provide sufficient liquidity for the company to meet its obligations. That sentence is what a company writes when the going-concern question was live and management resolved it by pointing at the asset sale. If the sale slips materially, the sentence has to be rewritten.
- Cash is thin: $37.9 million unrestricted at 31 March 2026, with $189.6 million restricted.

Run the value the other way and the picture is stark. Because the claims are so large, the equity behaves like a call option on the multiple applied to the operating businesses. Capitalising the $278 million target and deducting $2.38 billion of debt and a $1.42 billion preferred claim across 118.2 million shares: at fourteen times the shares are worth about $0.76; at fifteen times about $3.13; at sixteen times about $5.50; at seventeen times about $7.87; at eighteen times about $10.20. Every single turn of multiple is worth roughly $2.35 a share. On today's actual earnings power -- roughly $198 million once the rail synergies and Jefferson contracts land but before Repauno produces anything -- the common is worth close to nothing at any conventional infrastructure multiple.

That is not defined risk. That is a leveraged option with an unbounded loss.

## 5. MANAGEMENT AND SPONSOR CREDIBILITY ON DELIVERY

The financing execution has been genuinely good, and it deserves credit: a bridge facility refinanced into a $1.35 billion term loan maturing February 2028 (at a punishing 9.75% coupon); the Wheeling & Lake Erie acquisition closed and the promised integration delivering, with rail earnings up 31% year on year in the first quarter of 2026; Long Ridge signed with Jefferies and Lazard advising and Skadden as counsel, a properly resourced process; $217.9 million of Jefferson 2024B revenue bonds refinanced on 1 July 2026 with a $230 million secured bridge loan from Jefferies Finance; and the $45 million Tidewater Logistics acquisition closed 29 June 2026.

The delivery on earnings has been considerably weaker. The first quarter of 2026 produced a net loss of $127.2 million and a loss per share of $1.32 against a consensus expectation near $0.35 -- a miss of a different order of magnitude, not a rounding error. Moody's rates the company B3 with a negative outlook. The equity has halved.

Two items deserve to be flagged as behaviour, not accounting. First, the Tidewater purchase was funded by upsizing the term loan -- adding parent-level debt during a quarter whose entire narrative was deleveraging. Second, the Jefferson refinancing did not remove a maturity; it moved $218 million from 2024-vintage bonds into a bridge loan due 30 June 2027. Bridges are meant to be crossed. This one has to be termed out inside twelve months.

## 6. RED AND GREEN FLAGS

Red flags: the stated downside floor of $3.90 broke in the last week of July 2026, with a new 52-week low at $3.71 and the shares falling into the catalyst rather than tightening toward it; preferred stock at the rail holding company that pays dividends in kind and compounds ahead of the common, with a redemption claim near $1.4 billion, more than three times the entire equity market value; negative book equity, and liquidity language in the filings that reads as going-concern doubt resolved by pointing at the pending sale; a first-quarter loss per share nearly four times the consensus expectation; new debt raised for an acquisition inside a deleveraging quarter, and a $230 million bridge loan due June 2027 still to be refinanced; nearly a third of the earnings target dependent on a construction project that does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027 and has never earned a positive dollar; an open regulatory protest with no approval order published as of 3 August 2026; and a downgrade to the strongest sell rating by Wall Street Zen on 21 July 2026, alongside a Citizens JMP target cut from $12 to $10 on 15 July 2026 with a positive rating retained.

Green flags: the agreement is definitive and binding, with a committed and well-capitalised counterparty visibly still building in the same direction; the buyer has already cleared its own bondholder-consent hurdle, removing one of the two ways this deal could have died on financing grounds; the rail business is performing, at $40.2 million of quarterly earnings, up 31% year on year, from assets that are genuinely scarce -- short-line and regional railroads are local franchises that cannot be rebuilt; the sale removes $1.16 billion of debt and about $30 million a year of interest; three analysts carry targets between $8.75 and $12, so the gap between price and published fair value is not our invention; and two dated information events sit immediately ahead -- second-quarter results after the close on 5 August 2026 and the buyer's results on 6 August 2026.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The language has shifted from building to selling. A year ago the story was a diversified infrastructure platform; today the same management describes a sequence of disposals with the proceeds pre-assigned to debt. The common dividend, held at three cents a quarter, is now a rounding error against a 9.75% term loan -- it survives as a signal to income holders rather than as a return of capital, and it is the cheapest thing on the balance sheet to cut if the timeline slips.

Note also what the deal does not do for the equity. FTAI Infrastructure is the seller here, not the target. There is no offer price for its shares, no arbitrage spread, and no bid underneath the stock. Selling shareholders in a seller-side transaction get the proceeds, not a takeout -- which is precisely why the shares can and did fall while the deal remained fully on track.

## 8. VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

Trajectory: turning. The company is mid-transformation from a levered infrastructure conglomerate into a freight-rail platform, and the transformation is being executed competently on financing terms and unevenly on operating results.

The single thing to weigh before sizing: this candidate was selected as a defined-risk special situation -- a live dated event with a floor underneath it. The event is live and binding; the floor is not there. The price has already traded through the level that was supposed to bound the loss, senior claims of roughly $3.8 billion sit ahead of a $441 million equity stub, and the value of that stub swings about $2.35 a share for every single turn of the earnings multiple applied to the operating businesses. The upside to $8 or $9 is arithmetically reachable, but only by capitalising an earnings target at roughly seventeen times -- a target whose largest component does not begin producing until the first quarter of 2027, after the event window shuts.

On the economic franchise itself: the railroads are a narrow but real moat -- regulated local franchises with switching costs that a competitor cannot replicate -- and there is no structural force eroding demand for freight rail or coastal terminals. The threat here is financial, not secular. But a narrow moat inside a capital structure this heavy accrues its value to lenders and preferred holders first, and to the common shareholder only after roughly $3.8 billion of claims are satisfied.

The honest characterisation is that this is a leveraged call option on infrastructure multiples with a real, dated event attached -- not an asymmetric, defined-risk trade. It should be sized as an option, or not taken until the regulatory approval and the actual cash application are on the tape.
